topics: GPU compatibility and driver matrix (NVIDIA Ampere/Hopper)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-01 15:00 PST | Duration 48m 
Attendees: Jordan, Priya, Miguel, Leah (Redwood) — Sophia, Arjun, Emily, Tom, Naomi (LumenBridge)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call. We're Jordan from Redwood, AE, Priya our systems engineer, Miguel on CSM, Leah from product. How are we doing?
[00:08] Sophia: Good, thanks. Hi, Sophia here, head of cloud partnerships at LumenBridge. We also have Arjun our infra architect, Emily from procurement, Tom and Naomi for security.
[00:16] Jordan: Great. The goal for today is quick intro, understand where LumenBridge is trying to place a GPU onramp for customers, and identify compatibility risks — drivers, telemetry, and contract/take rate expectations.
[00:28] Sophia: Yep, high level — we want to offer a managed onramp for enterprise customers that need GPU acceleration for LLM inferencing but want to buy through LumenBridge. We want to white-label or co-brand if possible, and also route customers to hosted or private installs depending on compliance.
[00:44] Priya: Cool. A couple clarifying q's — are you imagining LumenBridge running Redwood Dedicated in your own cloud accounts or selling a managed Redwood Private appliance into customer data centers?
[00:54] Arjun: Both, honestly. Primary model will be resale of hosted with LumenBridge-managed billing, but for regulated customers we need a private/VPN or on-prem option. We also need guidance on multi-tenant isolation and KMS integration.
[01:12] Miguel: That makes sense — Redwood supports Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private VPC/on-prem. We typically recommend Dedicated for predictable throughput and Private for regulated data.
[01:24] Naomi: On KMS — we need to be sure HSM-supported, customer-managed keys are an option. Auditors flag any provider-managed key stores.
[01:32] Leah: We have KMS integrations with major cloud providers and also bring-your-own HSM in our Private deployment; we can support CMKs in the private control plane. I'll follow up with the security doc.
[01:44] Tom: Also curious about driver versions and CUDA compatibility — many of our enterprise customers are locked to specific stack versions, e.g., CUDA 12.x vs 11.x and specific NVIDIA driver builds.
[01:55] Priya: Good point — our runtime supports Ampere and Hopper families; however, certain optimized kernels (tensor intrinsics) require newer drivers. We maintain a driver matrix and a recommended minimum. We'll send a compatibility matrix.
[02:09] Sophia: Do you do anything automatic for CUDA/MIG isolation? Some of our customers use MIG profiles heavily.
[02:15] Priya: We do support MIG but with caveats — performance per slice depends on kernel choices and sequence length. For high-concurrency smaller requests MIG can be beneficial; we can run a quick simulation to show throughput differences.
[02:29] Jordan: On the commercial side, what's the expected take rate and billing flow? Are you thinking resale with margin or referral?
[02:36] Sophia: Resale with margin model. We want predictable unit economics for customers and a clear markdown for LumenBridge. We'll need an SOW for pilot pricing.
[02:45] Miguel: We'll prepare a pilot pricing sketch. For pilots we typically lock a small dedicated capacity pool and measure tokens per second to extrapolate costs.
[02:55] Emily: Procurement will need a standard MSA, SOC2 attestation, and a data processing addendum. Also SLAs around latency.
[03:05] Miguel: We can share standard legal stacks and SOC2 docs. We'll also surface SLOs for latency under the Dedicated offering.
[03:12] Sophia: Great. On technical: one blocker we've seen in other partnerships is the requirement to run in air-gapped on-prem — can Redwood's Private package be fully air-gapped?
[03:21] Leah: Yes, we have an on-prem package that can run with the private control plane in a customer network; however, some features like automatic model catalog updates will need a controlled pipeline. We can support manual model propagation.
[03:36] Arjun: If we go that route we need clear documentation: how images are signed, transport for model weights, and the upgrade cadence.
[03:44] Priya: We'll provide a secure rollout pattern — signed images, artifact repo, and recommended window for kernel updates. We have notes on rollback strategies too.
[03:55] Sophia: Excellent. Can you talk about model quantization and any quality tradeoffs? Several customers will want 8-bit quantized variants to reduce cost.
[04:04] Priya: Sure — Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per model and workload. In our experience, 4-bit/8-bit quant can save 2–4x on cost but sometimes increases small hallucination rates on sensitive prompts; we surface regressions bound to a prompt set during rollouts.
[04:22] Tom: Do you have eval tooling for that? We need to show customers the before/after.
[04:27] Leah: Yes, we have an eval harness that ties into prompt sets and can produce regression alerts. We'll share a sample eval spreadsheet for pilots.
[04:36] Naomi: From a security perspective we need token-level audit logs and encryption in transit at rest. Also SSO—SAML or OIDC for admin access is required.
[04:47] Miguel: We provide audit logs and SAML SSO for workspace admins; logs can be forwarded to customer SIEMs. We'll include specifics in the security pack.
[04:57] Sophia: How about network routing — can we route traffic by policy, like by latency or tenant tier? We often want to route lower-tier customers to cheaper instances.
[05:08] Priya: Yes — smart routing policies exist. You can route by latency, cost, or any tag. Fallbacks are configurable when capacity is constrained. We'll demo the routing rules in the deep-dive.
[05:21] Jordan: Let's capture some success criteria for the pilot — latency p95 under X ms for short prompts, throughput Y tokens/s, secure key management, and a resale contract. Does that map?
[05:32] Arjun: Sounds right — I'd add deterministic cost model for customers (predicted tokens/month).
[05:37] Sophia: And a one-month pilot with 2–3 customer examples onboarded.
[05:43] Priya: For the bench plan I'll ask for typical prompt lengths, concurrency, and target QPS. That'll feed driver/kernel selection and batching.
[05:54] Tom: One more ops note — how do you handle KV cache and prefix caching? Some customers want session stickiness for chat histories.
[06:02] Priya: We have automatic prefix/KV caching and configurable TTLs. For session stickiness we can set routing sticky sessions or use a shared KV cache with encryption at rest.
[06:14] Sophia: Any restrictions on model types? We partner a lot with open models; customers will want to bring their own models too.
[06:21] Leah: BYO models are supported, but we run a vetting process for performance and compatibility, especially if customers demand low-latency kernels. We'll provide quantization and compilation guidance per model.
[06:34] Jordan: A quick note on billing flow — if LumenBridge resells hosted capacity the billing can be net-netized or via usage feeds. We have flexible billing connectors into billing systems.
[06:45] Emily: We'll need an EDI or billing CSV to ingest, and a purchase order workflow.
[06:50] Miguel: Noted — procurement we'll connect with our finance integrations team and share sample feeds.
[06:56] Sophia: Are there any live case studies of partners doing reseller models?
[07:02] Jordan: A few channel partners have reseller pilots; we can share anonymized metrics and a partner playbook.
[07:08] Sophia: Perfect.
[07:12] [Pause — quick side conversation about calendar scheduling and doc links]
[07:30] Jordan: Ok, next step — we should schedule a kernel/driver deep-dive with Arjun and Priya, and a security deep-dive with Naomi and Leah. Priya will lead the performance benchmark plan.
[07:41] Arjun: For the deep-dive I'd like to include a dev node with identical GPU type to our customer's fleet — we can provide the instance spec.
[07:50] Priya: That works. We'll ask for CUDA/driver versions and I'll correlate against our matrix.
[07:57] Jordan: Anyone have blockers to the pilot timeline? We're thinking a four-week pilot starting mid-November.
[08:04] Sophia: That timeline looks fine if we can get the legal and security packet first week. Procurement needs two business days to review SOW after we send it.
[08:14] Emily: We'll need pricing to complete PO, so getting the pilot sketch is priority.
[08:20] Miguel: I'll push a sketch within 48 hours after this call.
[08:25] Jordan: Great. I'll summarize and send meeting notes with links to the security doc, compatibility matrix, and bench template.
[08:33] Sophia: Thanks — also please add a line on co-branding guidelines, that's a marketing ask.
[08:38] Leah: Will do.
[08:42] [Crosstalk — minor audio dropouts, brief overlap]
[08:50] Jordan: Recap of action items: Redwood to share integration checklist, driver matrix, security pack; LumenBridge to provide pod spec, customer SKUs and compliance notes; Priya to draft bench plan. Schedule two follow-ups — kernel deep-dive and security deep-dive.
[09:06] Sophia: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:10] Jordan: Thanks all. Bye.

Links mentioned: security pack (link to /s/secure-pack — internal), bench template (drive link), partner playbook (link to /partners/playbook).

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabeling and phonetic errors; speaker turns sometimes condensed.
